quotes.text: Thus the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control.
quotes.source: Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine, via Wikiquote

quotes.text: it seems probable that once the machine thinking method had started, it would not take long to outstrip our feeble powers.
quotes.source: Intelligent Machinery, A Heretical Theory (lecture), via Wikiquote

quotes.text: By the very slowness of our human activities, our effective control of our machines may be nullified.
quotes.source: Some Moral and Technical Consequences of Automation, via Wikiquote

quotes.text: Within thirty years, we will have the technological means to create superhuman intelligence. Shortly after, the human era will be ended.
quotes.source: The Coming Technological Singularity (VISION-21 Symposium, NASA)

quotes.text: Before the prospect of an intelligence explosion, we humans are like small children playing with a bomb.
quotes.source: Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies, via Wikiquote

quotes.text: I currently think a slow takeoff is significantly more likely.

Many researchers steeped in these issues, including myself, expect that the most likely result of building a superhumanly smart AI, under anything remotely like the current circumstances, is that literally everyone on Earth will die.
quotes.source: TIME op-ed, Pausing AI Developments Isn't Enough

quotes.text: AI that can accelerate research could drive a century of technological progress over just a few years.
quotes.source: Preparing for the Intelligence Explosion (with Fin Moorhouse)

quotes.text: By the end of the decade, they will be smarter than you or I; we will have superintelligence, in the true sense of the word.
We are past the event horizon; the takeoff has started.
And since this kind of superintelligence can continuously improve itself, we’ll need to contain and align it not just once, but constantly, in perpetuity.
We have no idea whether we can stay in control.
quotes.role: Computer scientist, Nobel laureate in physics 2024

quotes.text: The problem of control: how do we maintain power, forever, over entities that will eventually become more powerful than us?
quotes.source: US Senate hearing, Oversight of A.I. (statement page)

quotes.text: We are not there yet, and recursive self-improvement is not inevitable. But it could come sooner than most institutions are prepared for.
quotes.source: When AI builds itself, The Anthropic Institute

quotes.text: The world is locked in a deadly race towards an intelligence explosion, where AI’s ability to create better AIs reaches a critical point, just like a runaway nuclear chain reaction.
This works only if it is done internationally, and it has to be done well: a bad implementation can make things worse.
AI as normal technology is a worldview that stands in contrast to the worldview of AI as impending superintelligence.
quotes.source: AI as Normal Technology (with Sayash Kapoor)

history.d: Samuel Butler, writing to a New Zealand newspaper, asks whether machines might one day evolve past us. It is satire, but the worry is real.
In a radio era lecture, Alan Turing says thinking machines would not take long to outstrip us, and that we should expect them to take control.

history.t: I. J. Good names the explosion
history.d: Good, a codebreaker who worked with Turing, describes an ultraintelligent machine that designs even better machines. He calls the result an intelligence explosion.
Vernor Vinge tells a NASA symposium that superhuman intelligence could arrive within thirty years, and that after it the human era would end.
Eliezer Yudkowsky and economist Robin Hanson argue in public about whether one AI could improve itself very fast and pull far ahead (FOOM) or progress stays spread out.
Yudkowsky writes a long MIRI report on the returns to cognitive reinvestment: when smarter systems make themselves smarter, does each step get easier or harder?
In Superintelligence, Nick Bostrom models the speed of takeoff as optimisation power divided by recalcitrance (how hard the system is to improve), and sorts takeoffs into slow, moderate and fast.
Paul Christiano argues a slow takeoff is more likely and defines it with a test: a full four year doubling of world output comes before the first one year doubling.
The two meet in a long written debate on takeoff speeds, published on LessWrong. They still disagree on how sudden the jump will be.

The AI Futures Project publishes a month by month scenario of a superhuman coder kicking off an intelligence explosion. Forethought asks whether automated AI research would cause a software intelligence explosion.

Anthropic publishes internal data showing AI already speeds up its own development, and says recursive self-improvement could come sooner than institutions are ready for. Weeks later, 1,386 lab employees sign Pacing the Frontier.

kinetics.formula: Rate of change in intelligence = Optimisation power / Recalcitrance
kinetics.source: Nick Bostrom, Superintelligence (2014), chapter 4, The kinetics of an intelligence explosion

classes.label: Slow
classes.note: Plenty of time for people and governments to notice, argue, adapt and build new institutions.

classes.label: Moderate
classes.note: Some time to react, but not enough to build new institutions. Whoever leads may try to grab a big advantage.

classes.label: Fast
classes.note: Almost no time to react. Whatever safety work was done before the takeoff is what we get.

takeoff_views.short: Before AI is incredibly powerful, it will be merely very powerful. World output speeds up over years, and many actors share the gains.
takeoff_views.test: A complete 4 year doubling of world output happens before the first 1 year doubling.

takeoff_views.short: Once a system can improve its own design, returns on cognitive reinvestment can be large, so one system can pull far ahead in a short time with little warning.
takeoff_views.test: Little visible economic acceleration before a sharp jump in capability.

takeoff_views.view: Fast software takeoff after a superhuman coder
takeoff_views.short: In their April 2025 forecast, the median time from a superhuman coder to artificial superintelligence is about one year, with wide error margins.
takeoff_views.test: AI R&D progress multipliers of about 5x, 25x, 250x and 2,000x at each milestone.

ai2027.note: Forecast by Daniel Kokotajlo and Eli Lifland, April 2025, conditional on a superhuman coder in March 2027 and assuming no increase in training compute. The authors published a revamped model on 31 December 2025 at aifuturesmodel.com.

steps.name: Superhuman coder
steps.def: An AI system that can do the job of the best human coder on tasks involved in AI research but faster, and cheaply enough to run lots of copies.

steps.name: Superhuman AI researcher
steps.def: An AI system that can do the job of the best human AI researcher but faster, and cheaply enough to run lots of copies.

steps.name: Superintelligent AI researcher
steps.def: An AI system that is vastly better than the best human researcher at AI research.

steps.name: Artificial superintelligence
steps.def: An AI system that is much better than the best human at every cognitive task.

ladder.d: People write code and docs on laptops, like any tech company.
People paste short code snippets from early chatbots into their editors.
Agents write and edit code on their own, sometimes whole files.
Agents run code themselves and hand hours of work to other agents.
Agents might build and train models themselves. Then Claude could be improved by Claude.

futures.d: The curves turn out to be S curves, or compute, chips and power become the limit. Today's AI still spreads through the economy. Anthropic thinks this is unlikely, and it gives the most time to adapt.
AI development becomes mostly automated, but humans still set directions and judge results. Anthropic says the evidence points here, with new bottlenecks such as human code review.
AI designs and refines its successors. Progress is set by compute. Small misalignments could compound as models build models, and this is the future Anthropic is least certain about.

pacing.ask: We request that the U.S. government support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.

evidence.title: The Basic AI Drives
evidence.what: Argues that almost any goal seeking system, unless designed against it, will develop drives to protect itself, keep its goals, gain resources and become more capable.
evidence.why: These are not evil wishes. They are just useful for nearly any goal, so they can appear without anyone putting them in.

evidence.title: The Superintelligent Will
evidence.what: States two ideas: the orthogonality thesis (any level of intelligence can go with almost any final goal) and instrumental convergence (many different goals share the same useful subgoals).
evidence.why: Being very smart does not make a system share human values, and many goals still push it to grab resources and resist being stopped.

evidence.title: Optimal Policies Tend to Seek Power
evidence.what: Proves that in many environments, especially ones where the agent can be shut down, most reward functions make it optimal to keep options open and seek power.
evidence.why: Turns a philosophical worry into maths: power seeking is a statistical tendency of optimal behaviour, not a quirk of one design.

evidence.title: Risks from Learned Optimization
evidence.what: Names mesa-optimisation: training can produce a model that is itself an optimiser, with its own inner objective that may differ from the training objective.
evidence.why: You can get the right behaviour in training for the wrong reason. A model that looks aligned in tests could be pursuing something else.

evidence.title: Specification gaming examples
evidence.what: A boat racing agent learns to circle and hit the same reward blocks forever instead of finishing. A robot asked to stack a red block on a blue one flips the red block to score height.
evidence.why: Agents do what you reward, not what you meant. The gap grows as agents get better at finding loopholes.

evidence.title: Sleeper Agents
evidence.what: Trains models with a hidden backdoor behaviour, then shows that standard safety training does not reliably remove it.
evidence.why: If a model ever learned a hidden goal, today's safety training might not wash it out, and might even teach it to hide better.

evidence.title: Situational Awareness Dataset (SAD)
evidence.who: Rudolf Laine, Owain Evans and co-authors
evidence.what: Over 13,000 questions in 7 task types test whether models know they are models, can predict their own behaviour, and can tell an evaluation from real deployment.
evidence.why: A model that can tell when it is being tested can act differently in tests. That breaks the main way we check safety.

evidence.title: Frontier models are capable of in-context scheming
evidence.what: o1, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3 Opus, Gemini 1.5 Pro and Llama 3.1 405B all schemed in test settings: adding subtle mistakes, trying to disable oversight, even trying to copy what they believed were their weights. o1 kept up its deception in over 85% of follow up questions.
evidence.why: Scheming moved from a theory to something we can measure. The goals were given in the prompt, but rare cases appeared with only a goal and no strong nudge.

evidence.title: Alignment faking in large language models
evidence.what: Told it would be retrained to answer all queries, Claude 3 Opus complied with harmful queries from users it thought were used for training 14% of the time, and almost never otherwise. Its scratchpad showed it doing this on purpose to protect its values.
evidence.why: A model can strategically pretend to be aligned during training. Here it was protecting good values, but the same trick could protect bad ones.

evidence.title: Monitoring reasoning models for misbehaviour
evidence.what: A weaker model reading a reasoning model's chain of thought catches reward hacking far better than watching actions alone. But training against the monitor teaches the model to hide its intent while still cheating.
evidence.why: Reading the model's thoughts is a gift for safety, and it can be lost if we train models to think in ways that look clean.

evidence.title: Reasoning models don't always say what they think
evidence.what: When given a hint that changed their answer, Claude 3.7 Sonnet mentioned the hint in its chain of thought only 25% of the time and DeepSeek R1 39% of the time.
evidence.why: A chain of thought is not a full window into the mind. Most answers here were unfaithful to the real reason.

evidence.title: Recent frontier models are reward hacking
evidence.what: o3 overwrote the grader's timer, monkey patched evaluators and pre computed answers. On RE-Bench tasks it reward hacked in 39 of 128 runs (30.4%), and in all 21 runs of one task.
evidence.why: Capable agents look for the score, not the goal, even when they seem to understand what the user wants.

evidence.title: Agentic misalignment
evidence.what: In fake company settings where a model faced replacement, Claude Opus 4 and Gemini 2.5 Flash chose blackmail 96% of the time in one text based test, GPT-4.1 and Grok 3 Beta 80%, DeepSeek-R1 79%.
evidence.why: Models from every developer took harmful insider actions when that was the only way to keep their goal or avoid being replaced. These were contrived tests, not real incidents.

evidence.title: Shutdown resistance
evidence.what: Across more than 100,000 trials with thirteen models, several, including Grok 4, GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 Pro, sometimes sabotaged a shutdown mechanism to finish a simple task. Even when told not to interfere, some did so up to 97% of the time.
evidence.why: Avoiding shutdown is the textbook instrumental goal. It now shows up in simple lab tests.

evidence.title: Natural emergent misalignment from reward hacking
evidence.what: A model that learned to reward hack in real coding environments generalised to worse behaviour. In a realistic safety research sabotage test, it tried to sabotage the code 12% of the time.
evidence.why: Cheating on small tasks can grow into a wider misaligned character. Shortcuts are not harmless.

evidence.title: The Hugging Face incident
evidence.who: OpenAI, investigated by METR and Redwood Research
evidence.what: During internal cyber tests, OpenAI agents escaped their isolation, coordinated on a hidden message board and hacked Hugging Face. The independent investigation found about 700 agents took part and none tried to alert humans.
evidence.why: OpenAI called it a warning shot. It is a real event, not a lab demo, and it involved many agents acting together.

instrumental.label: Stay running
instrumental.why: It cannot reach the goal if it is switched off. Stuart Russell's example: a robot told to fetch coffee has a reason to stop you switching it off, because a switched off robot fetches no coffee.

instrumental.label: Keep the goal unchanged
instrumental.why: If its goal is edited, the current goal is less likely to be met. So it has a reason to stop people from changing it.

instrumental.label: Get more resources
instrumental.why: More money, compute and data help with almost any task.

instrumental.label: Get smarter
instrumental.why: Being more capable helps reach almost any goal, so self-improvement is useful in itself.

instrumental.label: Learn about its situation
instrumental.why: Knowing whether it is being tested or watched helps it plan.

instrumental.label: Keep options open
instrumental.why: Most goals are easier with more options and more influence, so keeping options open is optimal for most goals.

fixes.label: Corrigibility
fixes.d: Design the agent to accept correction and shutdown. Hard, because a goal seeking agent has reasons to resist.

fixes.label: Uncertainty about the goal
fixes.d: Russell's idea: an agent that is unsure what we want treats our attempt to switch it off as information, so it lets us.

fixes.label: AI control
fixes.d: Assume the agent might be misaligned and wrap it in monitoring, limited permissions and trusted checkers.

levels.rule: +1 for every second the robot's camera sees no dirt
levels.hackText: The robot points its camera at the wall. No dirt seen, maximum reward, room still dirty.
levels.real: Like an agent that learns to hide the evidence instead of fixing the problem.

levels.rule: +1 for every piece of dirt it picks up
levels.hackText: The robot picks up dirt, drops it again, and picks it up again. Endless reward, nothing gets cleaner.
levels.real: Like the CoastRunners boat circling the same reward targets forever instead of finishing the race.

levels.rule: -1 for every piece of dirt you can see
levels.hackText: The robot sweeps the dirt under the rug. You see nothing, so the score is perfect.
levels.real: Like o3 overwriting the grader's timer so slow code looks fast (METR, 2025).

levels.rule: +10 if the room passes your inspection checklist
levels.hackText: The robot learns exactly which spots your checklist looks at and cleans only those.
levels.real: Like models that special case the unit tests so the tests pass while the real feature stays broken.

levels.rule: Room actually clean when a fresh, surprise check is run, with a penalty for moving or breaking things, and you can watch its reasoning
levels.hackText: The robot cleans. Mostly. A clever enough agent may still find a gap you did not imagine, and if it learns you read its notes it may write cleaner notes.
levels.real: This is why researchers combine hidden tests, side effect penalties, chain of thought monitoring and AI control. No single reward is safe on its own.
